newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Telecom pact talks get boost from new offers.
newsitem.headline: Telecom pact talks get boost from new offers.

text.p: Efforts to shape a global pact opening up the $600 billion basic telecommunications market were boosted on Monday by offers from three new countries, including key hold-out Malaysia, trade officials said.

The new offers -- which list how far a country is ready to open up its domestic telecom sector to outside competition -- were formally tabled at a World Trade Organisation (WTO) meeting just five days from the February 15 accord deadline.
"This is very encouraging. It does look a lot better," said Neil McMillan, British chairman of the negotiating group for the long-delayed accord.

But McMillan, recalling the collapse of an earlier bid to get a deal before a similar deadline last April when the United States decided openings pledged by emerging Asian economies were not sufficient, declined to say if he was optimistic.
"We have come a long way. But it is up to delegations to decide whether it's good enough," he said.
Joining Malaysia in tabling their own offers were Ghana and the Caribbean island of Grenada.
Trade sources said an improved offer from Brazil, a big player in the global industry, was expected shortly.

With the latest three a total of 57 offers have been tabled, ensuring that a pact would cover much of the world's basic telecom sector, outside the two vast potential markets of Russia and China which are not yet WTO members.
But U.S. officials caution that it is "quality, not quantity" of offers that count, and say a "critical mass of quality" must be achieved.

They gave no immediate response to the Malaysian package, which provides for a maximum of 30 per cent foreign ownership of local companies in the sector, but there were signs this would not be enough to satisfy Washington.

The United States, which accounts for some 50 per cent of the world's telecom market, says access for outside companies must be at a good enough level to justify throwing open its domestic sector to all comers.
The European Union (EU), which like the United States tabled an improved offer last November, may table a final package on Tuesday or Wednesday, diplomats said.
One senior EU negotiator insisted on Monday that complaints from Washington over omitting mention of video services in its November offer were based on a misunderstanding.

EU officials say they believe they have convinced their key partners that commitments to allow such services are covered by other global agreements under the WTO's overall accord on trade in services, GATS.
Diplomats say another problem could be Canada, which has submitted a new offer but is insisting that foreign equity holding in Canadian companies cannot be more that 46.7 per cent.
The United States and the EU have been looking for more than 50 per cent. Both powers are also looking for better offers from Japan and South Korea.
